issues.legal_issue: A constitutional writ is not the proper means to reopen a completed voluntary purchase contract in order to recover part of the price while retaining the property.
material_facts: The purchasers applied for flats after receiving brochures that stated the prices and terms of allotment.
They paid the stated prices, took possession, and sought a partial refund without offering to return the flats.
There was no allegation of a false or incorrect statement or fraudulent concealment in the brochures.
issues.conclusion: The Court considered a writ petition an improper remedy for reopening the completed contracts to recover part of the purchase price, although it examined the petitions on their merits rather than rejecting them on the preliminary objection.
issues.legal_principle: In the contractual field, rights and obligations are ordinarily governed by the valid contract unless a statute confers a distinct power or obligation; Article 14 does not provide a means to avoid voluntarily incurred contractual obligations. The Court relied on Radhakrishna Agarwal v. State of Bihar and Har Shankar v. Deputy Excise and Taxation Commissioner.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_petition and voluntary_purchase_contract_completed and purchaser_kept_property and sought_partial_price_refund

predicates.constitutional_writ_petition: A person brought a constitutional writ petition seeking relief concerning a purchase contract.
predicates.voluntary_purchase_contract_completed: The purchaser voluntarily accepted the offered price, paid it, and completed the purchase.
predicates.purchaser_kept_property: The purchaser retained the property received under the contract.
predicates.sought_partial_price_refund: The purchaser sought to recover part of the price without returning the property.

issues.definition: When a purchaser uses a constitutional writ to seek a partial refund after voluntarily completing the purchase and retaining the property, the writ is not a proper means to reopen the contract.

issues.legal_issue: Different prices for public housing do not violate equal treatment where pricing distinguishes projects and reflects relevant differences, without unequal treatment among allottees in the comparable project class.
material_facts: The purchasers compared surcharge-bearing flats with flats in other schemes or at other times, including flats in an area where construction costs were higher because of rocky land.
The Authority’s pricing factors included land, materials, labour, transport, land availability, supervision, and management, which varied by time and place.

The surcharge was applied to the relevant schemes to help reduce the cost of housing for lower-income groups, while allottees in the comparable project class were not shown to have received unequal treatment.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the comparison across income groups alone was insufficient: a relevant pricing class could be defined by income group, area, time, and scheme, and the challenged pricing did not establish discrimination within that class.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits unequal treatment within a class unless justified by a valid classification; persons similarly situated must be assessed in relation to the purpose of the classification. Executive price fixation allows wide discretion, and courts do not ordinarily review economic pricing mechanics absent statutory control or patent hostile discrimination. The Court relied on Prag Ice & Oil Mills v. Union of India, Avinder Singh v. State of Punjab, State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills, and East India Tobacco Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh.

rule.if: public_housing_price_equality_challenge and project_specific_pricing and relevant_costs_vary and not unequal_treatment_within_comparable_project

predicates.public_housing_price_equality_challenge: A purchaser challenged different prices charged for housing provided by a public authority.
predicates.project_specific_pricing: The authority set prices by reference to distinct housing projects or schemes.
predicates.relevant_costs_vary: Relevant land, construction, labour, transport, or management costs differed between projects, locations, or periods.
predicates.unequal_treatment_within_comparable_proj: Allottees in the same comparable project class were treated differently in price without justification.

issues.definition: Different project prices do not establish an equal-treatment violation when relevant costs vary and comparable allottees are not treated unequally.

issues.legal_issue: An overall no-profit-no-loss policy does not require every individual flat or housing scheme to be sold at its own cost price.
material_facts: The purchasers argued that the Authority’s stated no-profit-no-loss approach required each flat to be sold at its individual construction cost.
The governing regulations defined disposal price by reference to the price fixed by the Authority and contained no formula requiring each flat or scheme to be priced at cost.
The Authority described its policy as applying to its overall housing operations, and the record showed that its housing work was in overall deficit.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that no-profit-no-loss did not have to apply separately to each flat, scheme, or developed parcel, and that the regulations did not prescribe a per-flat cost-price formula.
issues.legal_principle: The Delhi Development Authority (Management and Disposal of Housing Estates) Regulations, 1968, including regulation 2(13), did not prescribe a no-profit-no-loss formula for determining each disposal price. The Court treated the policy as an overall operating approach rather than a rule requiring cost-price sale of every unit.

predicates.public_housing_no_profit_no_loss_claim: A purchaser relied on a public authority’s no-profit-no-loss policy to challenge a housing price.
predicates.no_binding_per_unit_price_formula: The governing rules did not require each unit or scheme to be priced according to a prescribed cost formula.
predicates.policy_applies_to_overall_operations: The policy concerned the authority’s overall housing operations rather than each individual unit or scheme.

issues.definition: Where the policy concerns overall operations and no binding unit-by-unit cost formula exists, the policy does not require every unit to be sold at its individual cost.

issues.legal_issue: A surcharge is not shown to be arbitrarily calculated when the record connects the disposal price to revised project costs and an identified price benchmark.
material_facts: Revised estimates for a housing project reflected substantial changes from the initial estimates as actual costs emerged.
A government department accepted an offer to acquire flats at a stated price, which the Authority used as a starting point for determining disposal prices.
The Authority said the additional amount would help reduce prices for lower-income housing, and the evidence placed the challenged prices in proximity to the relevant estimated costs.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the contention that the surcharge calculation was arbitrary or irrational on the record before it.
issues.legal_principle: Price determination involves economic and technical factors for which the executive has wide discretion; courts are not expected to substitute their own price mechanics for those of the relevant experts absent a sufficient showing of arbitrariness. The Court relied on Prag Ice & Oil Mills v. Union of India and its discussion of executive price fixation.

rule.if: public_housing_surcharge_challenge and revised_cost_estimates_considered and accepted_price_benchmark_used and disposal_price_connected_to_project_costs

predicates.public_housing_surcharge_challenge: A purchaser challenged an additional amount included in the price of public housing.
predicates.revised_cost_estimates_considered: The authority considered revised estimates reflecting costs as the project progressed.
predicates.accepted_price_benchmark_used: The authority used a price accepted for comparable flats as a benchmark.
predicates.disposal_price_connected_to_project_cost: The evidence connected the disposal price to project costs and the stated use of the additional amount.

issues.definition: A challenged surcharge is not shown to be arbitrary when revised costs and an accepted price benchmark support the disposal price.

issues.legal_issue: The authorised officer could determine disposal prices, and the record showed approval of the price that included the challenged surcharge.
material_facts: The regulations permitted the Vice-Chairman to administer them and allowed the Authority to delegate regulatory powers to the Vice-Chairman or a whole-time member.
The Authority had delegated powers concerning disposal prices, and its resolutions recorded that delegation and the use of scheme savings to subsidise lower-income housing.
A price-setting note was approved by the Financial Advisor and countersigned by the Vice-Chairman.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the delegation challenge failed and that the record did not support the contention that the Vice-Chairman had not approved the disposal price, including any surcharge component.
issues.legal_principle: Regulations 3 and 59 of the Delhi Development Authority (Management and Disposal of Housing Estates) Regulations, 1968, read with section 59 as discussed in the judgment and the Authority’s resolutions, permitted delegation of disposal-price powers to the Vice-Chairman. The Court also considered the relevant resolutions and the Vice-Chairman’s countersignature on the price note.

predicates.public_authority_disposal_price_set_by_d: A public authority’s disposal price was fixed through an officer exercising delegated authority.
predicates.governing_rules_allow_delegation: The authority’s governing rules permitted the relevant pricing power to be delegated to that officer.
predicates.delegated_officer_approved_price: The officer’s approval appeared on the record for the price charged.

issues.definition: When the governing rules allow delegation and the authorised officer approved the price, the delegation and price approval are sufficiently authorised.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that a surcharge generated a large profit is not established where the evidence shows that the authority’s overall operations were in deficit.
material_facts: The purchasers asserted that the Authority had made a large profit by collecting the surcharge.
The parties disputed figures relied on by the purchasers, and the Authority’s evidence showed that its overall housing operations were deficit-ridden.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the claim that the Authority had made a large profit from the surcharge.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the disputed figures and the evidence about the Authority’s overall financial position, finding no support for the alleged large profit.

predicates.public_housing_surcharge_profit_claim: A purchaser claimed that an authority made a large profit by collecting a housing surcharge.
predicates.evidence_shows_overall_operations_in_def: The evidence showed that the authority’s overall relevant operations were in deficit.

issues.definition: A claim of large profit from a surcharge is not established when the evidence shows that the authority’s overall operations were in deficit.
